source.title: SeqGPT: An Out-of-the-box Large Language Model for Open Domain Sequence Understanding
source.authors: Tianyu Yu; Chengyue Jiang; Chao Lou; Shen Huang; Xiao-Bin Wang; Wei Liu; Jiong Cai; Y. Li; Ying-Hui Li; Kewei Tu; Hai-Tao Zheng; Ningyu Zhang; Peng-Jun Xie; Fei Huang; Yong Jiang

record.file_problem: The paper text is substantially complete. A local file path and some PDF layout artifacts appear in the text, but the paper is readable.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures held-out downstream NLU task performance across model sizes, a different measure from the pretraining-loss scaling laws. It reports its own size-sweep results bearing on V6, but does not test the original pretraining-loss laws.
record.gate_note: The paper reports downstream task scores by model size, so these are rows for V6. It does not report held-out pretraining cross-entropy, compute-optimal allocations, architecture comparisons at fixed parameter count, or fitted scaling-law predictions. Related power-law claims in the introduction and references are background citations, not results from this study.
record.test_reason: The paper runs its own model-size sweep (BLOOMZ backbones 560M–7B1, each trained with the same SeqGPT recipe) and reports held-out and held-in downstream NLU scores by size (Table 2, Fig. 4, Sec. 3.4.1). This bears on V6 in a new setting: instruction-tuned models fine-tuned for NLU. It is T3 rather than T2 because it does not target the scaling question with an alternative method. It fits no predictive curve and does not relate scores to pretraining loss. No other version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that larger backbones improve both held-in and held-out performance, with diminishing gains (the 3B→7B1 gap is much smaller than 560M→1B7). They also conclude that performance rises logarithmically with the number of training tasks/datasets, and that adding data volume without diversity does not consistently help. They fit no loss power law.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains and evaluates SeqGPT for downstream NLU benchmark scores across backbone sizes; it does not measure language-model held-out cross-entropy or fit the original scaling-law relationships.
record.method_sensitivity: The held-out task-specific scores vary by task: ID, NLI, RE, SF and SA are non-monotonic across the tested SeqGPT sizes, although the ALL aggregate rises.

fits_no_version.finding: Held-out performance rises logarithmically with the number of fine-tuning datasets, across all four model sizes (Fig. 5). Increasing samples per dataset does not consistently help (Fig. 6).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Downstream NLU performance after multitask fine-tuning grows roughly log-linearly with the number of fine-tuning tasks/datasets, not with data volume per task.

record.problems: The relevant scaling evidence is downstream task performance rather than pretraining loss; the study reports no fitted predictive scaling curves or uncertainty estimates for the size-sweep scores. The paper notes a large held-in/held-out performance gap and diminishing gains at larger model sizes.
record.rows_left_out: Table 2 reports task-by-task scores for the BLOOMZ baselines and SeqGPT without pre-training, and additional per-task results for those variants are not extracted; only their ALL scores are included here. Figure 6 also plots performance against samples per dataset, but its figure-only curves are omitted. The size-sweep results for standard SeqGPT are included for every task metric in Table 2.

untested.parts: Whether downstream gains follow a fitted, predictable curve. Whether downstream performance tracks pretraining loss. Only four sizes are tested, with no extrapolation.
Not tested: no pretraining loss is reported.
Not tested: no shape comparison at fixed size.
Not tested: fine-tuning scores by size are reported, but no power-law form is fitted.

missing.what: Held-out performance against number of training datasets, for each model size (figure only). It also shows larger models staying above smaller ones at every dataset count.

record.verdict_notes: Each row is one point in a four-size sweep, so its state describes the trend of its sweep. The four sizes are 560M, 1B7, 3B and 7B1. Training hyperparameters are fixed across sizes (4000 steps), so data and compute are not scaled with parameters. Scores average Micro-F1 and ROUGE over 48 sampled records per dataset, and no uncertainty is reported; small non-monotonic dips may be noise. The per-task scores without pre-training data are declared in rows_left_out. They are also non-monotonic for SA (71.2, 78.5, 76.0, 73.5) and SF (66.1→65.4 at 1B7).

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute.
Whether power laws fitted to small runs predict loss for much larger runs.
Compute-optimal parameter/token allocations and their relationship to compute.
Comparisons of depth, width, or other architectures at fixed parameter count.
Power-law behavior in other modalities or training regimes.
The paper tests held-out NLU benchmark performance across model sizes, but does not fit a predictive scaling curve or test downstream performance as a function of pretraining loss.
Dependence of pretraining-loss exponents or compute-optimal allocations on fitting choices and training setup.

relationships.condition: SeqGPT aggregate held-out ALL score, with and without the ChatGPT-generated pre-training data, plus held-in performance
relationships.reason: ALL rises monotonically with size: 57.2→65.5 with pre-training data and 53.9→65.4 without; the text says held-in also rises (r1-r8, r53-r56).
relationships.display_finding: Aggregate held-out scores increased monotonically from 57.2 to 65.5 with generated pretraining data and 53.9 to 65.4 without it, with gains also reported on held-in evaluations.

relationships.condition: SeqGPT held-out CLS, EE, MRC, NER and ET tasks
relationships.reason: Each of these task scores rises monotonically across 560M–7B1 (r13-r20, r25-r32, r49-r52).
relationships.display_finding: Every specified task score increased monotonically across models from 560M to 7B1.

relationships.condition: SeqGPT held-out ID, NLI, RE, SF and SA tasks
relationships.reason: These scores are non-monotonic in size. For example, SA peaks at 1B7 (77.2) and NLI drops from 62.5 at 3B to 58.9 at 7B1, so per-task gains are not reliably predictable (r21-r24, r33-r48).
relationships.display_finding: Task scores varied nonmonotonically: SA peaked at 77.2 for 1B7, while NLI fell from 62.5 at 3B to 58.9 at 7B1.

relationships.condition: Un-adapted BLOOMZ backbones evaluated with the SeqGPT prompt format
relationships.reason: Without task-format training, scale yields only tiny gains near the floor (ALL 3.6→6.2), and NER stays at 0.0 at every size (r9-r12).
relationships.display_finding: Aggregate performance rose only from 3.6 to 6.2, while NER remained at 0.0 across all sizes.
